definition: The exterior path-vector routing protocol of the Internet, which exchanges routes between autonomous systems over TCP port 179 and chooses paths by policy.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 9: Wide Area Networking

definition: Cisco-developed advanced distance-vector, or hybrid, routing protocol that uses the Diffusing Update Algorithm for fast convergence inside one autonomous system.
source: CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 3: Network Addressing, Routing, and Switching

definition: Open-standard link-state interior routing protocol that floods link-state advertisements and runs Dijkstra's algorithm to find the lowest-cost path, with no hop limit.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 9: Wide Area Networking

definition: Oldest distance-vector interior routing protocol, which uses hop count as its only metric, allows at most 15 hops, and sends its whole table every 30 seconds.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 9: Wide Area Networking

definition: Any routing protocol used by routers inside one autonomous system, such as OSPF, EIGRP, or RIP.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Glossary; checked against Chapter 9: Wide Area Networking

definition: Any routing protocol that exchanges routes between different autonomous systems; BGP is the only one still in use.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Glossary; checked against Chapter 9: Wide Area Networking

definition: A group of networks run by one organization under one routing policy, identified on the Internet by a globally unique number that BGP uses.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Glossary; checked against Chapter 9: Wide Area Networking

definition: Routing where an administrator types each route into the table by hand; simple and predictable, but it cannot adapt to link failures or topology changes.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 9: Wide Area Networking

definition: Routing where routers use routing protocols to share route information and build their tables automatically, rerouting around failures without manual changes.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 9: Wide Area Networking

definition: Type of routing protocol where each router periodically sends its whole table to direct neighbors and rates routes by distance, such as hops; RIP is an example.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 9: Wide Area Networking

definition: Type of routing protocol where each router floods advertisements about its own links so every router builds a full map of the network; OSPF is an example.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 9: Wide Area Networking

definition: Type of routing protocol that mixes distance-vector behavior with link-state features, such as sending updates only when something changes; EIGRP is the usual example.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 9: Wide Area Networking

definition: The time it takes all routers to learn about a topology change, such as a failed link, and agree on updated routing tables.
source: CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 3: Network Addressing, Routing, and Switching

definition: Loop-prevention rule where a router never advertises a route back out the interface from which it learned that route.
source: CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 3: Network Addressing, Routing, and Switching

definition: Loop-prevention method where a router does advertise a route back toward its source, but with an infinite hop count so it is treated as unreachable.
source: CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 3: Network Addressing, Routing, and Switching

definition: Number from 0 to 255 that rates how trustworthy a route source is; when two sources offer the same route, the router uses the one with the lower value.
source: CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 3: Network Addressing, Routing, and Switching

definition: In route selection, the number of leading network bits in a route entry, written as a slash value such as /24; more bits mean a more specific route.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 9: Wide Area Networking

definition: Route-selection rule where, if several table entries match a destination address, the router forwards using the most specific entry, the one with the most network bits.
source: CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 3: Network Addressing, Routing, and Switching

definition: Value a routing protocol calculates for each path from factors such as hops, bandwidth, or delay; among routes learned the same way, the lowest value wins.
source: CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 3: Network Addressing, Routing, and Switching

definition: Number of routers a packet passes through to reach a destination; RIP uses it as its only path measure and treats 16 as unreachable.
source: CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 3: Network Addressing, Routing, and Switching

definition: Router or firewall function that rewrites private IP addresses to public ones, so internal hosts can share registered addresses and stay hidden from the Internet.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 3: Addressing

definition: Form of address translation where many internal hosts share one public IP address, each session told apart by a unique port number in a translation table.
source: CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 3: Network Addressing, Routing, and Switching

definition: Translation that permanently maps one private IP address to one dedicated public IP address, so an inside server can always be reached at the same public address.
source: CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 3: Network Addressing, Routing, and Switching

definition: Translation that gives each internal host a public address from a pool on a first-come, first-served basis, so its public address may change each session.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 3: Addressing

definition: Translation that changes the destination of inbound traffic sent to a public IP address into the private address of an inside host, such as a web server.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 3: Addressing

definition: General name for protocols that let several routers share one virtual default gateway address, so hosts keep working when the active router fails.
source: CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 3: Network Addressing, Routing, and Switching

definition: Open-standard gateway redundancy protocol where routers share a virtual IP address that points to one master router, with the others on standby as backups.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 9: Wide Area Networking

definition: Cisco-proprietary gateway redundancy protocol with one active router, one standby router ready for automatic failover, and any other routers only listening.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 9: Wide Area Networking

definition: Cisco-proprietary gateway redundancy protocol that spreads traffic across all routers in the group, weighted by priority, instead of using one active router.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 9: Wide Area Networking

definition: An IP address not tied to one physical interface, shared by a group of devices for high availability, such as a gateway address that several routers back up.
source: CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 3: Network Addressing, Routing, and Switching

definition: Logical interface created on one physical router port, each with its own IP address and VLAN tag, and named with a dot number such as fastethernet0/0.10.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 8: Network Segmentation

definition: Design where a single router port, split into one logical interface per VLAN and connected to a switch trunk, routes traffic between the VLANs.
source: CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 3: Network Addressing, Routing, and Switching

definition: Logical Layer 3 interface on a multilayer switch with an IP address for one VLAN, often used as that VLAN's default gateway.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 8: Network Segmentation

definition: Forwarding traffic between different VLANs at Layer 3, done by a router or Layer 3 switch, because hosts in separate VLANs cannot reach each other directly.
source: CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 3: Network Addressing, Routing, and Switching

definition: Logical group of switch ports that forms its own Layer 2 broadcast domain regardless of physical location, separating traffic as if on separate switches.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 8: Network Segmentation

definition: Storage on a switch, such as the vlan.dat file on Cisco devices, that holds VLAN numbers and names apart from the running configuration.
source: CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 3: Network Addressing, Routing, and Switching

definition: On an 802.1Q trunk, the one VLAN whose frames cross without a tag; both ends must agree, and it should be moved off VLAN 1 for security.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 8: Network Segmentation

definition: VLAN set aside for IP phone traffic so calls are kept apart from data traffic and can be given priority for low latency.
source: CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 3: Network Addressing, Routing, and Switching

definition: Preconfigured VLAN, VLAN 1 on Cisco switches, that holds every port at first and cannot be renamed or deleted.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Glossary; checked against Chapter 8: Network Segmentation

definition: VLAN used only for administrative access to switches and other network devices, kept apart from user traffic and moved off the default for security.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 8: Network Segmentation

definition: Cisco-proprietary protocol that copies VLAN additions and changes from one switch to the other switches in the same domain over trunk links.
source: CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 3: Network Addressing, Routing, and Switching

definition: Switch port that connects one end device, such as a PC or printer, and carries untagged traffic for a single VLAN.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 8: Network Segmentation

definition: Switch port that connects to another switch or a router and carries traffic for many VLANs, marking each frame with its VLAN number.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 8: Network Segmentation

definition: IEEE 802.1Q method of inserting a 4-byte field with a VLAN ID into an Ethernet frame header so switches on a trunk know which VLAN it belongs to.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 8: Network Segmentation

definition: Combining several physical links between two devices into one logical link for more total bandwidth and automatic failover; member ports must match in speed and duplex.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 7: Network Architecture

definition: IEEE 802.3ad (now 802.1AX) protocol that lets two devices negotiate and manage bundled links automatically, adding or dropping member ports as needed.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 7: Network Architecture

definition: Windows feature that combines two or more network adapters in one host into a single logical adapter for failover and load balancing.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 7: Network Architecture

definition: Mode where a link sends and receives at the same time in both directions, the default for modern switch ports and NICs, with no collisions.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 5: Cabling

definition: Mode where a link can send or receive but in only one direction at a time, like a walkie-talkie, so collisions can occur on shared media.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 5: Cabling

definition: Mode where signals travel in one direction only, like broadcast radio, so the receiver can never answer on the same channel.
source: CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 5: Cabling Solutions and Issues

definition: Ethernet feature where two connected ports exchange their abilities and pick the best speed and duplex mode they both support.
source: CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 5: Cabling Solutions and Issues

definition: Interface setting for the data rate of a switch port or NIC, such as 100 Mbps, 1 Gbps, or 10 Gbps; both ends must match or negotiate it.
source: CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 5: Cabling Solutions and Issues

definition: IEEE 802.1D Layer 2 protocol that finds redundant paths between switches and blocks some ports so only one loop-free active path exists.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 7: Network Architecture

definition: IEEE 802.1w update to the original switch loop-prevention protocol that recovers from link failures far faster, often in milliseconds instead of tens of seconds.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 7: Network Architecture

definition: Largest packet payload, in bytes, a link can carry without breaking it up; the standard Ethernet value is 1500 bytes.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 4: Protocols

definition: Ethernet frame carrying more than the standard 1500-byte payload, often up to about 9000 bytes, used in storage networks; every device on the path must support it.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 4: Protocols

definition: Splitting a packet larger than the outgoing link's size limit into smaller pieces, each with its own header, which adds overhead and slows delivery.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 4: Protocols

definition: A numbered slice of a Wi-Fi frequency band that an access point and its clients agree to transmit on; in the United States each standard slice is 20 MHz wide.
source: CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 6: Wireless Solutions; CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 6: Wireless Networking

definition: The amount of spectrum, in MHz, that one Wi-Fi transmission uses, such as 20, 40, 80, or 160 MHz; wider means more data but fewer free channels.
source: CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 6: Wireless Solutions; CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 6: Wireless Networking

definition: Combining two or more adjacent 20 MHz Wi-Fi slots into one 40, 80, or 160 MHz slot to raise throughput, best done in the less crowded 5 GHz band.
source: CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 6: Wireless Solutions; CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 6: Wireless Networking

definition: Wi-Fi frequency slots far enough apart that their signals do not interfere, such as 1, 6, and 11 in the United States 2.4 GHz band, assigned to neighboring access points.
source: CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 6: Wireless Solutions

definition: Rules set by national agencies such as the FCC on which Wi-Fi frequencies, slots, and power levels may be used; they vary by country and shape outdoor 5 GHz designs.
source: CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 6: Wireless Solutions; CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 6: Wireless Networking

term: Spectrum and Transmit Power Management Extensions
definition: The IEEE 802.11h amendment for the 5 GHz band that adds radar detection and automatic power reduction so wireless LANs meet regulations, especially in Europe.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 6: Wireless Networking; CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 6: Wireless Solutions

definition: An 802.11h feature that makes an access point watch its 5 GHz slot for radar, stop transmitting there when radar appears, and tell its clients to move to another slot.
source: CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 6: Wireless Solutions; CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 6: Wireless Networking

definition: An 802.11h feature that lowers an access point's radio output on a 5 GHz slot to reduce interference and tells clients the power limits that apply to the network.
source: CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 6: Wireless Solutions; CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 6: Wireless Networking

definition: An access point feature that directs dual-band clients toward the faster, less crowded 5 GHz band, for example by answering their probe requests only on that band.
source: CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 6: Wireless Solutions; CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 6: Wireless Networking

definition: The configurable name of a wireless network; a client must be set to the same name as the access point before the two can communicate.
source: CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 6: Wireless Solutions; CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 6: Wireless Networking

definition: The unique identifier of one access point radio, normally its MAC address, which tells apart the access points that share one wireless network name.
source: CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 6: Wireless Solutions; CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 6: Wireless Networking

definition: The network name shared by every access point in one larger wireless LAN, so clients see a single logical network and can move between access points.
source: CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 6: Wireless Solutions; CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 6: Wireless Networking

definition: A single access point together with the wireless clients associated with it, the basic building block of an infrastructure wireless LAN.
source: CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 6: Wireless Solutions; CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 6: Wireless Networking

definition: Several access points that share one network name and form one larger wireless network on a single subnet, letting clients roam between them.
source: CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 6: Wireless Solutions; CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 6: Wireless Networking

definition: An access point setting that announces the wireless network name in beacon frames so clients can find it; turning it off hides the name but does not secure the network.
source: CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 6: Wireless Solutions

definition: A wireless design in which every node relays traffic for the other nodes, so data finds alternate paths when one node fails and coverage extends over a wide area.
source: CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 6: Wireless Solutions; CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 6: Wireless Networking

definition: A peer-to-peer wireless network in which a few nearby devices talk directly to each other with no access point; the IEEE calls it an independent basic service set.
source: CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 6: Wireless Solutions; CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 6: Wireless Networking

definition: The most common wireless LAN design, in which clients connect only through access points that bridge them to the wired network and control their access.
source: CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 6: Wireless Solutions; CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 6: Wireless Networking

definition: A dedicated radio connection between exactly two endpoints, usually with focused antennas, used to join two buildings or as a long-distance backhaul.
source: CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 6: Wireless Solutions; CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 6: Wireless Networking

definition: An access point set up to join two separate networks, or two remote parts of one network, over a radio link; its throughput demand is higher than a normal client's.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 6: Wireless Networking

definition: The wireless security standard that replaced the first WPA, encrypting traffic with AES through CCMP and offering a Personal passphrase mode and an Enterprise server mode.
source: CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 6: Wireless Solutions; CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 6: Wireless Networking

definition: The 2018 wireless security standard that replaces the WPA2 passphrase handshake with SAE, requires at least 128-bit AES, and better protects management frames.
source: CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 6: Wireless Solutions; CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 6: Wireless Networking

definition: The WPA3-Personal handshake in which client and access point both prove they know the password, resisting offline dictionary attacks and giving forward secrecy.
source: CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 6: Wireless Solutions; CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 6: Wireless Networking

term: Counter Mode with Cipher Block Chaining Message Authentication Code Protocol
definition: The WPA2 protocol that uses 128-bit AES with a 48-bit initialization vector to give both encryption and message integrity, replacing the older TKIP.
source: CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 6: Wireless Solutions; CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 6: Wireless Networking

definition: Wi-Fi authentication in which every user enters the same passphrase, which the network uses with its name to make the encryption keys; the mode most home networks use.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 6: Wireless Networking; CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 6: Wireless Solutions

definition: Wi-Fi authentication in which each user signs in with personal credentials checked by a central server, usually RADIUS through 802.1X and EAP, instead of one shared passphrase.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 6: Wireless Networking; CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 6: Wireless Solutions

definition: A separate wireless network name and passphrase that gives visitors Internet access while keeping them isolated from the organization's internal devices and data.
source: CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 6: Wireless Solutions; CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 6: Wireless Networking

definition: A web page that a new client on a visitor network is redirected to, where the user must log in or accept the terms of use before getting Internet access.
source: CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 6: Wireless Solutions; CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 6: Wireless Networking

definition: A setting that lets a wireless client reach only the default gateway and the Internet, blocking it from talking to other devices on the same network.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 6: Wireless Networking

definition: An antenna that sends and receives with roughly equal strength in all directions, giving wide 360-degree coverage but a weaker signal and shorter range than a focused type.
source: CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 6: Wireless Solutions; CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 6: Wireless Networking

definition: An antenna that concentrates its signal in one direction for a stronger link and longer range, used for point-to-point links between buildings or through obstacles.
source: CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 6: Wireless Solutions; CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 6: Wireless Networking

definition: An antenna's strength compared with a theoretical isotropic antenna, measured in dBi; roughly every 3 dB more doubles the effective power output.
source: CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 6: Wireless Solutions

definition: An access point that works on its own and is configured one at a time through its own web page or command line, with no central controller.
source: CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 6: Wireless Solutions; CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 6: Wireless Networking

definition: An access point that hands configuration, firmware updates, RF tuning, and roaming control to a central wireless LAN controller; used in large enterprise networks.
source: CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 6: Wireless Solutions; CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 6: Wireless Networking

term: Control and Provisioning of Wireless Access Points
definition: A protocol that lets a central wireless LAN controller manage lightweight access points by tunneling their wireless frames to the controller with extra headers.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 6: Wireless Networking

definition: The central wiring room or rack of a site, holding the core routers and switches and usually the demarc, with backbone cables running out to every other wiring closet.
source: CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 8: Network Operations; CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 2: Infrastructure and Documentation

definition: A secondary wiring closet, at least one per floor or building, connected to the central wiring room by backbone cable and feeding cabling to nearby work areas.
source: CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 8: Network Operations; CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 2: Infrastructure and Documentation

definition: The point where the service provider's network ends and the customer's network begins, which marks who is responsible for each side of the connection.
source: CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 8: Network Operations; CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 2: Infrastructure and Documentation

definition: The standard measure of equipment height in a rack, 1.75 inches; a common full-height rack holds 42 of them, and a 1U switch fills one.
source: CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 8: Network Operations; CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 2: Infrastructure and Documentation

definition: The dimensions of an equipment rack: a standard 19- or 23-inch mounting width, a height counted in units such as 42U, and a depth that varies by maker.
source: CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 8: Network Operations; CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 2: Infrastructure and Documentation

definition: Switch airflow in which warm air leaves through the side with the network ports, so the ports face the hot aisle; the less common option.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 2: Infrastructure and Documentation; CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 8: Network Operations

definition: Switch airflow in which cool air is drawn in through the side with the network ports, so the ports face the cold aisle at the front of the rack.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 2: Infrastructure and Documentation; CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 8: Network Operations

definition: A data center layout in which rows of racks face each other front to front over cool-air vents and back to back over rows that carry heated exhaust away.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 2: Infrastructure and Documentation

definition: A rack cabinet, or a storage box mounted in a rack, with a locking door that stops unauthorized people from touching the equipment inside.
source: CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 8: Network Operations

definition: A rack- or wall-mounted panel of RJ45 jacks that terminates many horizontal cable runs in one place so short cords can connect them to switches.
source: CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 8: Network Operations; CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 2: Infrastructure and Documentation

definition: A cabinet or rack enclosure that provides space to terminate, splice, and store fiber-optic connections, the optical counterpart of a copper jack panel.
source: CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 8: Network Operations

definition: Cabling from a wiring closet to the wall jacks on the same floor, up to 90 meters of permanent run plus patch cords for 100 meters in total.
source: CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 8: Network Operations; CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 2: Infrastructure and Documentation

definition: Cabling, often fiber, that connects the entrance facility, the main wiring room, and the per-floor closets, including the runs between floors.
source: CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 8: Network Operations; CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 2: Infrastructure and Documentation

definition: A battery unit between the wall outlet and equipment that keeps devices running through an outage long enough for an orderly shutdown and smooths power fluctuations.
source: CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 8: Network Operations; CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 12: Performance and Recovery

definition: A battery backup that feeds equipment from the wall outlet and switches to battery only after it senses a power loss, leaving a brief gap.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 12: Performance and Recovery

definition: A battery backup that always powers equipment from its continuously charged battery, so there is no switchover gap and noise, surges, and sags never reach the device.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 12: Performance and Recovery

definition: A rack-grade power strip that carries power from an outlet, battery backup, or generator to many devices; intelligent models add remote metering and outlet on and off control.
source: CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 8: Network Operations; CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 12: Performance and Recovery

definition: The total power that a device, rack, or site draws, measured in watts or volt-amperes (about 1.4 VA per watt), used to size battery backups and circuits.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 12: Performance and Recovery

definition: The electrical pressure of a power feed, measured in volts, which must match the equipment rating and stay steady; spikes, surges, and sags are changes in it.
source: CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 8: Network Operations; CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 12: Performance and Recovery

definition: A fuel-driven machine that produces electricity to keep a site running through a long utility outage, after battery backups carry the load for the first minutes.
source: CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 8: Network Operations; CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 12: Performance and Recovery

definition: An inexpensive device between an outlet and equipment that sends excess voltage from spikes and surges to ground so it does not reach the device.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 12: Performance and Recovery; CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 8: Network Operations

definition: The moisture level of a data room's air, best kept at about 45 to 55 percent relative; drier air builds static, damper air causes condensation and corrosion.
source: CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 8: Network Operations; CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 2: Infrastructure and Documentation

definition: How hot or cold a data room is, best held at about 20 to 25 degrees Celsius (68 to 77 degrees Fahrenheit) by dedicated cooling to prevent equipment overheating.
source: CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 8: Network Operations; CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 2: Infrastructure and Documentation

definition: Equipment that detects and puts out fires at building, room, or rack level; data centers often use gas or foam instead of water so electronics are not damaged.
source: CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 1: Introduction to Networking; CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 8: Network Operations

definition: A nonconductive gas fire suppressant, such as FM-200, that stops a fire by absorbing heat or lowering oxygen and leaves no residue, so equipment is not harmed.
source: CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 8: Network Operations; CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 1: Introduction to Networking; checked against CompTIA Network+ Practice Tests: Exam N10-009 (Zacker) – Chapter 2: Network Implementation

definition: An older gas fire suppressant that leaves no residue on equipment but is no longer installed because of the harm it does to the ozone layer and climate.
source: CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 8: Network Operations

definition: The building system that moves, heats, and cools air; data rooms often get their own separately managed unit to keep heat-sensitive equipment within its operating range.
source: CompTIA Network+ N10-009 Exam Cram (Dulaney) – Chapter 8: Network Operations; CompTIA Network+ Guide to Networks (West), Cengage – Chapter 2: Infrastructure and Documentation
